reasoning: Both outputs correctly diagnose the sibling-module coupling (direct import + in-constructor instantiation of billing's PostgresInvoiceRepository), explain the same core downsides (untestable without a real DB, coupling to billing's storage internals, breakage on billing-side refactors), and both supply a complete, concrete code fix (port interface, refactored NotificationService, composition-root wiring, and a mock for tests). The two solutions are very close in quality, but B is marginally stronger on both architectural correctness and thoroughness. B enumerates three distinct problems (sibling coupling, inconsistent DI between the two constructor dependencies, and the absence of a port for what 'overdue invoices' means to the notifications module) versus A's two. More importantly, B places the new port inside `modules/notifications/ports/`, i.e. the port is owned by the consuming module and billing's adapter satisfies it structurally from the outside — this is the more idiomatic Ports & Adapters arrangement (the module that needs a capability defines the port; other modules provide adapters for it) and it fully severs notifications' compile-time dependency on anything under `modules/billing/*`, including billing's domain layer. A's fix has the port live in `modules/billing/domain/...`, which is a legitimate 'billing exposes a port' pattern but still leaves notifications importing a billing-owned file. B also adds a forward-looking design note (a thin anti-corruption adapter in `modules/notifications/adapters/` if billing's row shape ever diverges from the port), showing deeper consideration of long-term boundary integrity. A's discussion is very good too and its aside referencing 'this codebase's container.reviewRepo pattern' is a nice contextual touch, but it is speculative/unverified against the actual file under review and adds less concrete value than B's anti-corruption-layer guidance. Overall B is the more complete and architecturally precise review, though the margin over A is not large.
